blocks.x: I'll give your name Mr. Penn, your full name and we'll get started. My name is Samuel Penn. Do you have any middle name? Samuel Euless Penn. When were you born, if you can give us your birth date.
Well I was born on September of 1902.

About the same age as Manuel Paul, is that right? When were you born Manuel? 1904. Four, when you were younger. Manuel Paul is here tonight too. We're over at Sammy's house. Ralph Collins, this is Bill Russell. So we have all the names on here for identification. Can you tell us what part of the state you were born in Sammy?
I was born in Louisiana.
Which town? Morgan City, Louisiana. Did your folks play any music? Your mother or father?
No, none of my people played no music. I was the only one in the family.
No brothers or sisters that played anything either?
No brothers.

Can you remember what the music was like over there? Because we hear a lot of it about, we talk to everyone from New Orleans, but what kind of music was over in Morgan City? I've never heard much about it. Any bands over there?

Well, we had a band that I first started playing in. The manager was named Jake Johnson. At that time we were playing, but it wasn't a Dixieland music. We was playing swing music, but it wasn't Dixieland music.
What were you playing, Sammy? From sheet music? Or how were you playing?
Yes, we were playing sheet music and then playing Viya too. Oh, I see.
Well, what instrument did you start on?
Well, I started to playing drums. When I was twelve years old in Morgan City, Louisiana, I started to playing drums.
Do you remember where you got your first drums, what they were like?
Well, the first drums that I played on, Mr. Bill, it was a tub, an ordinary tub.
Like a watch tub?
Watch tub. Yeah.
What kind of drumsticks did you have?

Well, we had some drumsticks was made for me to use. Mr. Jake Johnson made a pair of sticks for me. And I had one of those round kegs that cheese used to come in. For snare drum. That was my first set I started on.
Was it a little low cheese box? That's right, it was a little low cheese box. About a six inch box like that? That's right, sir.
Size of a snare drum.
That's right, sir.
That's the way I started.
Well, what did you beat on? Did you have a skin across it or something?

No, it had snares on it and it had some kind of a little, well it wasn't a skin, it was some kind of a tissue like that. But it was a hard tissue, you couldn't bust it. Some kind of plaster like it was. Yeah. Something on a, like a thin raincoat cover like that. Oh yeah, something like that. But it had snares on it, we could play. Yeah.
That sounds pretty good.
At that time.

At that time. Put the snares on the same head that you beat on? No, on the other side. Right on the other side of that, yeah. That's right. Like two heads on it. That's right. But you mean, were the snares on the same? The snares was on the side with the cover like a thin rain. Yeah, but you only had the one cover. Was the back of it still wood or open? The back, the front of it was wood. Wood, yeah. That's right. Oh, that's right. Did you have any lessons when you started out or pick it up yourself?
No lessons at all, the more than Jake Johnson, the manager, tried to teach me how to play drums.
Yeah.
And from that on, well, I just kept on playing tubs around there until I got a set of drums.

Do you remember any of the other bands when you were even a little kid, six or seven years old when you first started in school? What kind of music did they have around town? Do you remember any? Well, I don't remember, Mr. Bill. Think at all?
No, not at all at that time.
Were there any brass bands in the town that they ever had a parade?
Yes, sir. We had a few fellas there and we used to make up a brass band between the ones that was in Morgan City at the time.

The fellas, they didn't come from New Orleans, they were right there. Right there in Morgan City. Somebody knocking on a shut-up. Okay, we're talking about the brass band, you say the people there in town got together for a brass band sometime too?

We used to go to Boybick, Louisiana, that's across the river from Morgan City. And between the two towns, Morgan City and Boybick, we used to make up a brass band. That's the only way they had a brass band in Morgan City at the time.
About how big was it, do you remember?
How big the band was? Well, Mr. Bill, we used to have around eight, seven and eight fellas playing music at that time.
Remember what instruments they would use on the street?
Well, yes, I do. They used to use clarinet, two trumpets, trombone, and baritone I think you called it, that's right.
Yeah, baritone and pulling.
Yeah, so far as I remember.
Yeah, I know it's hard to remember every little detail. So just whatever you can think of is good.
Yeah, so far as I can remember that.
They have a bass drum and snare drum both? Yes, they had bass drum and snare drum.
Two drummers. Yeah, I used to play snare drum.
How old would you be about then, Sammy? Well at that time I was somewhere around about thirteen years old.
Oh, I see, yeah.
And were all the members of the band about the same age, about that age?
Well, yeah, we was all mostly at that time. Pretty young. Yeah.
And that was, as far as you know, that was about the first band that did that around there, was it?

Well, that was the first band because we used to go to other little towns from Morgan City, like Jennerette, Louisiana, and also Patterson, Louisiana. They didn't have any band at all. They used to get us to come down and play parades on holidays. Yeah, that's right. Which like Fourth of July and different days like that, you know? And you'd play parades? How about dances? Did you ever play any dances? Well, the band that I was playing with, with Jake Johnson, well we used to play dances then, with our orchestra, we had Morgan City.
Were there any other bands before that, do you think, that played for dances? When you were a kid did you ever hear them from outside even?

Well, I did used to hear a band by the name of Ezekiel Mack from Boybick, Louisiana. He had a nice band but he was an older man than I was. I was, well, too young to play in his band. But I used to go down and sit down and listen to them and sit in some time, well they told me I had to go home, I was too young to stay out late at night like that.
Coming back for a moment to that, Jake Johnson, you said about how old would he be?
Well, he was the oldest man in the band. He'd be a few years older than you? Oh, he might have been about five or ten years, about five or six years older than I was.
Is he still living, do you know?
No sir, he is dead now, Mr. Bill.
You say he made the drumsticks for you, can you remember how he made them or what material he made them from?

Yes, I was sitting down in the backyard, I remember that, me and him, and old chair rounds. He cut them out and made the round of a stick on the end just like a drumstick and sandpaper. Oh, we were about, to remember it, we were about most of half a day making those sticks.
What instrument did he play?
Well, he played bass, violin.
Bass, violin. Is there any relation, any chance, to the Toot Johnson? They were up in the Baton Rouge, I think, around there.
Yeah, I know him, but I don't think this Johnson was a relation to him at all. No, sir. But I know who you're speaking of, but there are no relations.
Well now, did he show you anything about the, you say you learned mostly about them from Jake Johnson, did he show you anything about the rhythms or the beats or anything or did you pick that up?

Well no, he didn't show me anything about that. He didn't know anything about that. I just picked that up from listening to that band that used to come around my home town, Morgan City. Before I left there I used to listen to them. And I just tried to play all the time when I hear other fellas play. I didn't get disgusted, I just kept on. And fellas would tell me, you're doing good Sam, you're doing good. Well that made me feel very good. And I used to go around different places and hear the bands.
Do you remember any of those bands, the names of them, or anybody in those bands that you heard?

Well the only one at that time, like I aforesaid, was Ezekiel Mack, and I was playing with Jake Johnson. And they used to have a band come from Crowley, Louisiana, but I just remember another fellas, it's been so long. It was two brothers had that band, but I know they had a good band, and I used to sit down and play with them when they come to Morgan City. They were just crazy about my playing, and I just liked to play with them because I didn't think I could make it with them.

What did that music sound like in those days? Was it anything like the, what they call usually Dixieland bands today? Anything like Kid Thomas' band, or any of the bands that we've heard in late years?
Well, Mr. Bill, I'll tell you the truth about it. I didn't know anything about no Dixieland until I come to New Orleans. I started playing here.
What did they call it? Any certain name, like a ragtime band?
Jazz, that's all they said, jazz music. That's all. They called it jazz music. Yeah, that's all. Yeah, but I know nothing about Dixieland until I come to New Orleans.
Most of the pieces, what type of pieces were they? Were they like one steps or foxtrots or two steps or what? Plenty waltzes or anything?

Well, plenty waltzes. They know it, plenty waltzes. They used to play foxtrots. Another old time dance they used to play. I just can't remember it now. They used to dance it all the time in those days. I just can't call a name of it.
How did they dance it? In couples?
Yes, in couples. Other words it's something like a card drill or something like that they used to play out there in the country.
Did you ever play any of those mazurkas or anything like that?

Yeah, I played some of that too in Burbick with the Ezekiel Max band. Oh yeah, he played those? Well he was a good musician. He was a reading musician? Yes. Otherwise he was a professional at that time. Oh I see. And he carried a nice line up. He carried a nice band.
Did you ever go ahead and take any lessons on any instrument later with a regular teacher?

Well, Mr. Bill, I did take lessons to play tramo on. But I got back on my drums. I liked it in my drums. This is in Morgan City? Yeah, in Morgan City. But I liked it in my drums and I just went on back and it's on my drums. I didn't stay off them that long. And I had an uncle in the country by the name of Chester Morrison. He bought my first set of drums for me.
Oh yeah.

And at that time they were really nice drums and I just thought the world of him for buying me a set of drums because I had none. And I kept those drums quite a while until after I made up my mind to come in the arms. Well now did you get your trambone before your set of drums? Well I got the trambone after. I got the drums first. You know old times drums were made. Then I liked it the way trambone, the fellow was playing trambone used to live beside me right next door to me. And I liked the way he used to play and I told him I wanted to play trambone. And I tried to play that. Which I imagine if I'd have stayed on it I'd have been a trambone player.
That was his trambone you were using? Yeah that was his. I never owned none. Well that explains why you sometimes pick up the trambone in Thomas' band. That's right. That's right.
We haven't seen you do that for about a year now. I forgot about it.
That's right. That's right. Well then after you'd borrowed this Foller's trambone it was after that that you got this Chester, did you say Chester Morris?
Chester Morris, that's right. Got you the drums? Yeah he bought a set of drums for me.
What kind of a set was it?

Well it was a good set he bought for me. It was a leaders. Did you? Yes he came down the audience and bought it for me and I still was in Morgan City. And they surprised me one night with a set of drums.
What all did you have? How big a cymbal or what kind of cymbals?

Well I had small cymbals and at that time they wasn't making the real large drums. And it was good drums, leaders. I think he must have, I bought them from war lines I guess, or either coins that were selling instruments those days too. And cymbals were small and also…
Did you have any wood blocks or cowbells?

I had all that Mr. Bill, all that, all that. Traps was just like the one we made but real traps these wasn't. See because the others we made it was made with wood and a piece of wire on it at the bottom that we could work the traps with you know. And a spring leading from the top of the tub on this pedal. Yeah I see. You had a homemade pedal there.
Yeah I had a homemade pedal. With the, what do you call it, overhead beater?
That's right, overhead beater. That's right. Oh it was, it was something to see. It was really, everybody liked it. Yeah, but it worked good. Yeah it did. It worked fine.
Well now this new set that you got from Chester Morris, did that have an overhead beater?

Well no. At that time it was a pedal but it was a different pedal from they got today because it was, it was made of nothing but like a tin light. It was very light. See? It wasn't made like the ones we got today with the two double sides or nothing like that. See just one, one, one straight beat. One hand. Yeah. One mall on it. Oh one mall. Yeah. And the ones we got now you know they got space you can change up if you want you see from one side to the other. Wasn't like that.
Did you have a cymbal fastened on your bass drum too, that little beater on the side on the cymbal with that?
I used to have a cymbal on the side when I played the trap that would hit the cymbal on the side see. Didn't have all the cymbals like we got now you know.
Did everybody use that with the foot too, the little cymbal with the foot?
The cymbal with the foot beats the cymbal and the bass drum at the same time. See.
Did you ever use the high hat or sock cymbal in those days?
No sir I never used it. I never did use nothing like that in those days. In fact I never saw, I never saw nothing like that till I came from New Orleans. Sock cymbals.
I was going to ask, did any of the New Orleans bands come over there on any special holidays or anything that you can remember when you were young?

Well I can't remember. A band used to come from New Orleans by a name, Jewel Barnes. He was a trammond player and he was a manager of the band. Used to come from New Orleans to play in Morgan City. Was that a dance band or a brass band? That was a good band. A dance? A dance band. And I used to sit around on the bandstand until I'd get a chance to try to play with the boys and sometimes he'd let me play. So he kept telling me, why don't you come to New Orleans? He said, you're too good to be out here. Jewel Barnes, then? Yeah, Jewel Barnes. So I said, oh I don't believe I want to come to New Orleans. Nah, I was doing alright out there. How old would you be about then? Well I was, I'd say, about eighteen years old, something like that. Well you'd been playing for a few years then. Yes, I had been playing, but I still wasn't out there in the country. I hadn't made up my mind to come here. So every time he would come to Morgan City he would always tell me, say, we're going to take you back with us, say you're too good to be out here. He let me play and they all would satisfy my playing. So I made up my mind to come to New Orleans. When I come down here I met him, and he was one of the first ones that was taking me around all the bands. I still played with him some down here in New Orleans. Then after that, uh...
Well wait a minute, how old would you be then when you did finally come here?

When I came to New Orleans, close to my remembers, I was around, uh... Oh, about twenty, twenty-two years old or something like that. To my remembers, I was about twenty-two years old when I come to New Orleans. And I got around plenty of bands but I was scared to play. They'd always want to hear me play, because Jewel told them I was a good drummer. You brought your drums down with you though? Oh yes. I brought my instrument with him. And after I played with him a while, and Jewel, and so he liked it to me and he wanted me to play regular with him. Well I didn't know whether I could play regular with him because I had talked with some other fellas about playing, and I didn't want to disappoint them, so I was Buddy P.
Where did you ever meet him? How did you happen to know him?

I met him through Jewel Barnes, the fella that asked me to come to New Orleans. I met him through him. And when I started playing with Buddy, well, I just thought I was alright then, so I just made up my mind to play music with any of the bands that wanted me to play until I got in a regular band.
Well in other words, Buddy Patek was the first band you played with regularly after you came down here.
Well Jewel was the first one. Jewel Barnes was the first one.

Well you did play with him? Yeah I played with him, I stayed with him about three years. Oh you did, I see. Then I went with Buddy. Well can you remember any of the other boys that were in Jewel Barnes' band at that time?
Well, most of them now is dead, but I do remember that Edwin Washington, you know Washington. Oh yeah, he was there. Big Washington. Big Washington. Yeah, Big Washington.
Played Algo those days?
Yes, he was playing to Incline it. Clarinet.
Clarinet.
And I'm trying to remember now, but it's been so long, I just can't remember all the first. I just can't recall.
What did Jewel's play did you say? Tramble. Oh that's right. You don't remember the trumpet player then?

Well Mr. Bill he did. Mostly it was a trumpet player I used to play with him, was Kent, not Chris Kelly. I just can't think of this man's name, he was a trombone player. He was a trombone player? That was his brother who used to play trumpet with Jewel. He was a trombone player.
Not uh, not uh. Johnson?
No, they used to have a song about his name.
But it had been Mutt Carey by any chance.

Mutt, that's who it was. Now that, Mutt Carey has got a brother by the name of Chris Kelly, not Chris Kelly. Jack Carey. Jack Carey, that's right. Jack Carey. You see I just can't think of those things like I was like. You mentioned the other night about Jack Carey, that's why I thought you met him. Yeah, yeah. Well that was uh, his trumpet player at that time.

Oh yeah, Mutt played there with Jewel Barnes and something. And uh, Zeb. Zeb used to play Kliney. Oh, do you ever remember any other part of his name? No, all I know was Zeb. All you knew was Zeb. Yeah.
How was he? Oh Zeb was a wonderful Kliney player, he was a fine fellow. And he could play too. Uh huh. Yeah.

Yeah. So it seems anybody ever knew him, but I was Zeb. Yeah, well that's all I knew. That's all I knew. Now was anybody else in the band you can remember? Like did you have a bass fiddle or a banjo or a guitar?
Yeah, they had a bass fiddle in the band. Jewel used to use a fellow by the name of Tom Harris. Oh, Tom Harris. Yeah, he was a bass player. He was a good bass player too. Now you know him well.
Oh yeah, I think you mentioned his name. He was in the picture. Was that the band, was that the band? Was that the band? Was that the man in the band? Let me see, we got about five.
Do you remember hearing that band, Manuel ever?
That band he's speaking of? Probably, yeah. But I can't remember. I don't remember exactly.
I don't remember exactly.

It'll be about a six piece band. The years that he's speaking of now, it was in my religious years. Oh yeah, about a six piece band. I can't call the banjo player's name. I forgot his name. Well then, go ahead.
I was going to say, tell us about, not Chris Kelly, but Buddy Petit, when you started working with him.

Well, when I started working with Buddy Petit, we used to play at the fairground here in New Orleans. That time, we used to have two bands there. I stayed with him quite a while. In fact, I was with him when he first took his stroke. First stroke he took. And we used to advertise in the streets and have fun all the time. At that time, we used to have plenty of bands in the street. We don't have that here in New Orleans no more. And, uh...
They have wagons or trucks in those days?

No, Mr. Bill, they used to have trucks. And you leave out on a Sunday morning at 11 o'clock, and get in the streets, you might meet two or three bands. And when you get on a corner and meet those bands like that, you couldn't get away. You just had to play. The best man wins.
But did you ever do any of that work before you went with Buddy? With Buddy Petit? Yeah, before you went with Buddy, like with Jules. Did Jules do any of that too, on the trucks?

Yes. Mostly all the bands I've played with since I've been young at that time, they used to advertise. All the dances would be given on a Sunday night like that, they'd advertise Sunday morning. It was wonderful.
Well, when you first went with Buddy there, who else was in his band, Sammy? Can you remember?

Well, uh, I can't recall all the fellas' names now because it's been quite a while, but they used to have a fella who played tramwain with us by the name of, um, it's in on Ramport Street, man. The old man used to play tramwain. He played brass band music too, he was well known. Carnish. Oh, yeah. Carnish. Oh, yeah. He used to play with us. And he's an old-time trombone player. He died, but he was good. He used to play in brass band music.
Now, uh, did you ever play with Frankie Dooson at any time? Do you remember Frankie Dooson on trombone?
No, I never played with him. I, uh, uh, Who'd he have on clarinet with him then at that time, uh, Sammy? Can you remember?
Yeah. I, I, I can't call this man's name. He used to live downtown and he died too. He used to play with Randy and then he used to play with, uh, Buddy Petit sometime. I can't call his name.
Wasn't there a fella named, Georgie Boy?

Well, Georgie Boy used to play with, uh, Buddy Petit. That's right. Yeah, Georgie Boy used to play with Buddy Petit. But it's another fella, I just can't call his name. It wouldn't, uh, it wouldn't be, uh, uh, either Frank Lewis or Willie Warner. Do you know those names? No. No. Yes, I know them. I know them. I just can't call his name right now.
Did Zeb ever play with, uh, Buddy Petit too, or not?

Well Zeb, mostly Zeb used to play with Randy sometime, and sometime he used to play with Buddy Petit. But, uh, he never did play in one study band. Zeb was a clarinet player, used to play with anybody that wanted to hire him. But he was a good clarinet player though. How did Buddy play? How was... Well Buddy played wonderful. Buddy was one of the best trumpet players on secondary that you had in New Orleans. For second trumpet? Yeah. And, uh, of course he's taken sick. And after he's taken his first stroke, well he couldn't play like he wanted to then he tried but he couldn't see. And we still travel together after he was sick, after he took his first stroke and got better we traveled.
Where did you all go? On the long trips or just...?
Well, uh, we went to Chicago and, uh, went to Texas and all about different places. I was with him when he took the last stroke he died in a cupboard. That's the way he died.
What kind of stroke did he have? Was he paralyzed or anything? Paralyzed stroke. Really bad.

And it hit him so he couldn't talk. Oh. Couldn't move at all? Well, a very little bit he did before he died after the second stroke. Uh huh. How did the first stroke leave him? In what... Well, it just, it left his hand in bad shape and his mouth was twisted just a little bit on the first stroke he had. And then, uh, but my mother after that, well, he could play. But he couldn't play like he would like to play, but he could play a little bit.
Do you know how old he was? Was he much older than you? I know...
Well, he was around, he was around the same age me and him was. It was a buddy petite. Yes. When he, when he died. Uh huh.
How long were you with him all together about Sammy? How many years?
Well, I don't know exactly. Uh, I, I, to my remembrance I stayed with him about five years.
Uh huh. Well, how long, uh, how long had you been with him before he had his first stroke?
Oh, I had been with him. In fact, I played with the band about, about three years and something before he had a stroke, because we used to travel together.
Uh huh. And then, uh, he had another one about two years after that? That's right. Uh huh.
Well, he wasn't very old when he died then, was he?
No, he wasn't too old when he died, Mr. Bill. He was still in his, uh, nice, uh, prime to play music and he was, he was a real good musician.
Well, you say he played second trumpet. Did he ever have another trumpet in the band with him?

Well, not when he'd have his own band, uh, he was traveling and he didn't have no other trumpet. But when he'd go play with other bands, like Kid Thomas sometimes, now he played with us over the river a long time. Oh, Buddy did? Buddy petite? Yeah. Oh, with Thomas? Yeah, he played over there and he'd play second.
Oh, I didn't know that.
That's right.
I heard Thomas talk about him being a wonderful second trumpet player. Yes, he was wonderful second. I didn't know he played the same band with Thomas.
That's right, he played with Thomas a while over there, a long time, the river at, uh, Spex.
That's right, I do say. You oughta know that. I remember watching him once before, yeah.
And then he played second and it was wonderful.
Uh huh. He had a pretty good execution, wouldn't you say?
Oh, yes, he could execute the trumpet. Uh huh. He had a real nice melody. He could play. And he was a wonderful player, a cornet player.
And he would, uh, he would, uh, sort of, uh, take off, get off on the melody sort of thing?
Oh, yes, he'd get off.
Was he a pretty loud tone or soft type of tone?
Well, uh, he was a, uh, a trumpet player or something like Punch. Yeah. Uh, nice soft melody, nice soft trumpet player, you know. Just at times he'd get up, get off, but he was very nice.
Did he ever use, uh, mutes? Uh, any kind of mutes?
Yes, he used plenty of mutes.
Uh, did he ever use his hat for the mutes?

No, uh. Did he use a regular mutes? Uh, uh, uh, never did. Sometimes he'd use a derby. See, he used to wear a derby. Uh huh. In fact, me and him both used to wear derbies. Yeah. And, uh, he'd take that derby and make some wonderful music out.
Would he hang it on the horn or just hold it?
No, he'd just hold it in front of the horn. Just hold it in front of the horn. Yeah, you don't see that much, but he really could play it, though.
You remember if he usually had a cornet, a short cornet or a long horn?
Yeah, well he had one, he had a cornet. A cornet. Not a long trumpet then? No, no, him and, uh, uh, Chris Kelly, that's what they used to play. Short horn, trumpet.
Yeah, yeah. Well, now, did he have the regular line of mutes besides that, or did he use a glass like Thomas sometimes used a glass?
No, I don't think he ever used a glass. Well, Thomas is about the only one I know picks up that glass and plays like that. Thomas has got some stuff with him with that glass.
Yeah, he used a, Buddy used to use the regular mutes. Yeah.
Did he ever use one of the rubber plungers, you know, the flushers?
Yeah, yeah, they used to use that too, Mr. Bill. Uh, the trammel players used to use it, and sometimes the trumpet player.
Yeah, yeah.
Did he ever have a way of, uh, I've seen some guys, sometimes they hold a mute and they sort of don't have it all the way in. Yeah. Sort of hold it, did he ever do that?
Well, no, I never did see Buddy do that. But I know, I'll tell you a fact about Rene, that's all he used to do, he was all kind of
mutes.
And hold it just like you speaking of. He was a mute player, he really could play with me.
Well, when did you go to Rene? Right after you left Buddy's band or?
Well you see, Rene had a brother who used to play drums with him.
Oh, I see.
And the only time I played with Rene is when his brother was sick of it, couldn't make
the job. Oh, I see, yeah.
Him and his brother stayed together for years, see. And that was the only time I played with him, he would sit and get me any time he needed
a drummer. Well what happened to Buddy's band after he took that second stroke? What actually happened with the band?

Well, what happened to the band, we just played a while and didn't get much work. What we used to get when Buddy was living. So the men began to drop out. In fact, Buddy was well known and Buddy used to get plenty of work. So after he died, the fellas just dropped out and got in other different bands. So that's why I went and started playing with Chris Kelly a while.
Oh, that was when you joined Chris Kelly. Yeah. From Buddy. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
You mentioned how you joined Chris Kelly after Buddy Petit died, then you joined Chris.
Yeah, I started playing with Chris Kelly and I liked to play with Chris because Chris used to advertise to play in the streets. And we used to meet plenty of bands in the
streets. Who else was in Chris's band? Can you remember who else played then? Well, I can remember a few minutes because, and some of the minutes I've told you about because...
We were talking about your singing. You say you used to sing all sorts of numbers. They

didn't carry a songster with you. Yeah, well I had to sing those days, Mr. Bill, because we had nobody to sing. And some of the numbers that Thomas thinks of and play, well I'll sing to them yet. I used to like to sing in a band. And I used to study all the-
We were talking about this picture. We saw this over at Manuel's place, this picture of Kid Thomas. Where was that taken again?
That was at the American Legion Hall.
In McDonnellville? That's McDonnellville. About when was that, would you say, Sammy? Before the war? Or during the war?
That was after the war.
After the war.
And all these musicians on here now.
This bass player, who's he again?
That's little Henry Rust, they call him. That's one of the bass players that used to play in the Navy band.
And the second trumpet, of course, isn't with the band.
Well, that's one of the Vinette brothers. They have a couple of them play music. Well, that's the trumpet player of the Vinette.
Yeah.
And the rest is Thomas, Big Wash. Now you got Joe James on piano. And Wash is on saxophone. And Manuel Paul, he's on sax. And Sam Pins is on the drums. And Thomas is on trumpet.
And then the bass player and the other trumpet player. Mm-hmm.

Now, that's when I had the other set of drums, Ralph, that you were speaking of. Yeah. Mm-hmm. That the rims. Mm-hmm. By beating on the rims. I even had to put a cloth on top of this tum-tum because it was too loud.
Yeah, I see you have a cloth on that. See? Mm-hmm.

And a lot of people used to see that on there and wondering why I put it on there. Some of them thought that if it was a bus I had to take it and show them, take it off and show them that it was too loud. That's why I used to carry that on there.
That's the one you had a light in, that bass drum.
Well, that's the one.
Mm-hmm. How did you get that light in? You made a little hole for it?

Well, no, it's easier to take down, take it down, and then it'd have a place for, you to set a light in it, you know? They had a place for them? Oh, yes, they got them in all bass drums mostly. Oh, they do? Mostly. Oh. On account of weather sometimes. If you catch a bass drum, it's a, anyway it gets kind of old, you don't have a light it won't come up to stand it at all. Oh, I see. You can't even screw it up there no more.
Oh.
And you have to have a light. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
It'll keep it sort of dry and warm. Yeah, that's right. That's right. Uh-huh.

Sammy, there's one thing you were talking the other night which, uh, seemed important to me. The, uh, down here we notice people away from New Orleans notice how the music, musicians play together better and the bands sort of stick together. And of all the bands here, we all say now that here your band, it's the, uh, best band around, it sticks together, they play together better. And that little story you told about the other day, we don't have to mention who it was that fired you and then how Kid Thomas says, well that's the end of the whole band. I mean, to me that seems important. It's an example of how you all, you're real pals, you stick together and play together. It is, it is. You can tell a little bit about that time, just remind us of that.

It, uh, it is wonderful. You see, uh, at those days, at that time we was playing regular. In fact we were playing too much for, in one place. It's like many hours, you started at two o'clock, was it in the afternoon? Yeah, we were working on Saturday nights, Friday nights and Saturday nights. Go right back on Sundays at two o'clock and play, uh, Sunday night right on, two. Well we had been doing that for quite a while. And they had a back hall every, every time we played that. And I was telling Mr. Bill, well I wanted to get off one night, you know, and so the man that runs the place wanted to, told Thomas, says, well, says if he goes and get off tonight, he can stay off. And so I kept packing my instrument up, because I was going, you know, I had to go. There was somewhere else I had to be. And I had to play it all day. It was time to knock off, and that night too, you know.
Was that one o'clock in the night about?

That was about the most one o'clock then. So Thomas told him, says, well, says, I'm sorry, say, if you let him go, say, you just want to let all of us go, you just want to get a band, say, because I don't see why you won't let him go, say, because he's got the goal, say, we're willing to play where I am and hold your people for you, say, but if you let him go, say, we're all going. Well, I wouldn't talk to him that night because I was kind of feeling hot over it, and I left, and he came by and talked to me.
Came back to your house?
He came by to the house and talked to me about coming back to Wake.
So the next morning was over here early?

So I told him, I says, well, I don't think I am coming back. So he says, well, I talked to Thomas already. He says, now I want to see what you say. I said, well, what did Thomas say? He said, Thomas says, whatever you do is all right. He says, if you come back he'll be glad. I said, well, I says, I want to talk to Thomas first. So I talked to Thomas and he told me, he says, well, if you want to go back it's all right. He says, we'll go back if you go back, if not we won't go back. So I told him, I says, well, I'll let you know. We may come back, I'll let you know. But he wanted to know that night, you know, that morning at least. But I didn't give him no answer to that until I finished talking with Thomas. So I told him, all right, I says, we coming back. So that's one thing about this band, all the years that we've been playing together, they're very nice about sticking with one another. Now that don't mean for no man to do wrong that we're going to stick with him. But if you do the right thing, Thomas certainly will stick right by you. He'll do that. He's a good leader. Oh yeah, she's fine. She's fine. To me that seems important.

I mean that helps explain why you all play so well together too. I mean you all work together in every way and stick together. That's right. It's a good unit. A lot of bands aren't that way. They're fighting amongst themselves.

Mr. Bill, I've heard other musicians say when we be out together sometime that Thomas has got a bunch of men that never augurs, have no trouble on the bandstand like some bands usually do, and we don't.

Actually I think most of the New Orleans bands in the past and even today are the same type. They stick together nice, but you notice that more here than in other parts of the country. That's right. I notice it being all over the country at times. That's right. It's one of the characteristics of our music here that the bands play better together for some reason. Oh yeah. That may be one reason.

Well I think it is, Mr. Bill. I think it is. Because you know if you're playing in a band and you've got a bunch of men, nice men, playing with you and been playing with you for years and they never have an argument or nothing like that, well it's just a pleasure to be playing together. Everything goes along easy. But if you try to kick on one man all the time and probably that man is doing all right, maybe you just don't like something about him, I don't know, but that makes the band bad. You always have to get somebody hiring different men. We don't have no trouble like that.

Some time ago, Mr. Bill, you asked me to Sam's question about that. Why is it that I seem to be more happier with Thomas than with the rest of the men? You asked me that. Well I feel very much there at home with him. You see, with that bunch of men. That's really why.

You can tell they all, like Sammy says, they all love music too. That's right, that's right. I always say that about Manuel too. He never puts his horn down. You can't stop him. Sometimes the band stops and he'll start all the piece by himself. He'll start all the piece by himself. He just won't stop playing.

He just loves music. He's ready, that's right. That's right. You take like Joe James. I like to hear Joe sing sometimes, but sometimes he won't sing when I want him to sing. He won't sing for me, you know. Just that time he feel good he'll sing. I like the way he sings.
I've only ever heard him sing the blues. Does he sing anything else?
Well, he used to sing a few numbers all the time, but he just lately just sing blues now. He's a blues singer.
I guess he's been feeling rather unwell. Yeah.
Well, he has been.
I believe that has plenty to do with it. Probably does. Yeah, it has plenty to do with it.

Well, I was going to ask one more thing about speaking of your drums and your drum style. Except for the little breaks you take and the endings, you don't hardly ever take a drum solo. In the old days, did they ever take drum solos? Like now they'll take, say, a cornet solo, trombone solo, a sax solo, a piano solo. In the old days, did they ever have drum solos? Like sometimes they do now.

No, they didn't have it in the old time, Mr. Bill. And you know, just recently now, since the band's been fluting so many other instruments, they're fluting drums now. And you catch some of the drummers, it's really nice the way they take their part. You didn't think that a drummer could play his part like they're doing now. Because they didn't give him the chance years ago. They didn't give him any chance at all. All he had to do was just play straight music, keep the time. But now they give you your part and you just play it.
Well did you take drum breaks in the old days like you do now with the Thomas band? I mean the whole band would stop and you'd take a break?
No, we never had nothing like that at that time.

I was going to ask, when did those endings sometimes, I know Baby Dodds, a drummer friend of mine up north who died last year, called those tag endings. You know when the band gets the end of the piece then the drummer plays four bars then they come in four more bars the whole band. When did that start down here? Do you remember? Did they do that in the old days?
No they didn't do that in the old days at all.

Baby told me he didn't hear it down here at all or even in Chicago only when he went to New York in the 40's that he first heard anybody do that. I wondered if you know, did you hear that before the war?
Well I heard it, the band I heard it from was Sharky. Sharky?
Yeah, yeah.
And that's where his drummer used to do that all the time. That's where I got it from.
He might have gotten it from New York too or someplace, I don't know where they got it.
Well he could have gotten it from New York. I don't know. But I used to hear that drummer play like that all the time. That's where I got it from.
But in the old days you never did that? No.
And then it ain't too good to use it too regularly. Now if you use it sometime it sounds alright.
Sometimes every piece they end that way and they'll put on three or four of those endings like they had two. It gets old.
That's right.
I wanted to ask you just a few more, one or two more things. We spoke about Buddy Petit and his style, Chris Kelly and his style. What about Kid René? We didn't say too much about his style.
Well, what I know about René, René, he had a different style of playing music. You know they had another band used to play in the city here. Newman's band.
Dwight Newman?
Yeah. What was his name? Creole Serenators.
Creole Serenators, yeah. Dwight Newman was the leader?

Now the Creole Serenators and René, those two bands, were the only two bands that would play different from the rest of the bands. Now René had a way of playing that nobody else used to play like. You could tell René that he was in the hall playing. You didn't have to go look in there, you'd know it was René, because he had a different way of playing. Just like the Creole Serenators. And that's another band that had a different way of playing.
What do you mean by a different way of playing?

Well they just played different from the way we play or any other band. They have a different way of playing. And you can tell it. Was it more jazzy or less jazzy? Well some people said it wasn't, and some people said it wasn't, but most of them said it wasn't, you see.
Did they have about the same kind of a line-up of the band though, same kind of pieces?

Well they had the same kind of line-up that we or any other band have. It's just the way they used to play was a little different, the way they had their band range and play their music was different. And René, the way he played trumpet, nobody else used to play no trumpet like him because it was just a different style he was playing in, but he could play.
Nobody had ever played much like him before you don't think?
No, not that I know. Not that I know. He's one man was a different trumpet player. And it was nice the way the people said it was.
I was going to ask if you could talk a minute about the Sam Morgan band. Did you hear that? What type band was that? I never got to hear them. They did make a couple of records.

Well Sam Morgan had a nice band. Sam Morgan and Celestine used to be the two of the best bands you had around here once. In fact I didn't hear him too much because after he died his brother taking it up. Well then they left and it was always over the lake somewhere. But at the time I did hear him, he had a good band. That's all you could hear them days was Sam Morgan and Celestine. They really had a nice band. Did you ever hear them play?

No, I never have. Never have played them. Somebody told me that Sam Morgan was about the first one or at least a lot of times he used to use a slapstick such as Manuel and Kid Thomas use quite often today. I wonder, did you ever play the slapstick too, Sammy?
No, I never did play it, Mr. Bill, but I think Chris Kelly was the first one started that.
You think Chris Kelly had one? He had one too? I didn't know.
That was the first man started it. With them sticks. That was the first man started it. Then it's Celestine. You remember when Celestine had it.
Oh yeah. And Chris Kelly, did Chris Kelly play it himself too?
Oh yeah, he used to set his trumpet down and start hitting them clefs.
What's the correct way to play those?
Well I never did play them, you know, Manuel played them. Manuel does alright. Thomas played them but I never did.
When did you start on that Manuel? Just with Kid Thomas? Just with Thomas, that's it.

I noticed he always seemed to clap on the second beat and the fourth beat. The off beat. Well, after beat most of the time. After beat most of the time. Do you find that helps your drumming style, Sammy?

Yes, I love it. I love it because it's a whole lot of help to me. And then if he's got the sticks, you know, slap sticks, well, then I can make my stuff like I want on my blocks and lightly on the snare drum, then it sounds fine.
And you still got the beat?

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And I like to hear Thomas play them too. Of course. See? And of course Thomas don't sing much but when he do sing it's really key. It's really key. Thomas sings sometimes and changes voice there and I'm telling you people just falls out.
Yeah, those, those, I hear him sing the Milk Cow Blues and the A-Lap Bar. Did he used to sing a lot of different stuff? He doesn't seem to sing too much.

No, he never just sing too much but yeah, Black Thomas used to make you fall out, always dressing up in different things. A little nightgown and a little hangout. Different things, yeah. All kinds of funny hats and oh, he come out with a dress on and all. People used to fall out, you know. He used to be a cowl girl, right? Yeah, he used to be cowl.
Yeah, he used to walk around with balance in a tray on his head once.

Yeah, that's right, that's right. Oh yeah, Thomas. And he used to get out off the bandstand and no care how big a hall was, his band would still be playing. And all I'd want to do just be so I could hear that trumpet, so I could keep the time. He used to get out off the bandstand and walk all around and sometimes you didn't know where he was going. He'd be all around outside and come through the back, but just so I could hear that trumpet. He's still playing his trumpet? Still playing his trumpet. Walked outside the hall.
He did it over to Tip Top about a year ago or so, yeah.

I don't remember going outside the hall. They went to New York Berry to play a dance once. And people was a little late coming in. And they was on the outside. Oh they had plenty of people on the outside. So Thomas said, I'm going to get them in here. Thomas started to blow, we was playing, Thomas started blowing his horn trumpet and went on the outside and went to the window each window and people started to run in there though. They really packed that hole that night. Thomas said, I was going to get them in here. See, all I had to do was just go to that window and play.
Blame through the window.
That's right. It's all just kicks.
Is there something else you had there?

No, there's one question I was going to ask about them. Do you remember anything about Buddy Petit's funeral? I understand they had a big funeral at that time. Yes. There was a lot of bands playing or something. Do you remember anything about it?

No, I left town, Mr. Bill. You weren't here? I remember that good. I was playing with somebody I had to leave that morning around ten o'clock. I heard about the funeral. But I was away with the band then. I can't remember. Yes, I can remember now. I was with, I made a trip with Randy because his brother couldn't go. I made a trip with Randy and we had to leave that morning. But I heard that they had a big funeral.
Did they bring him back to New Orleans, say, from Coverson?
That's his home, I believe, in Pulitzer.
Oh, oh.
His wife, I know his wife was from there.
What name again?
Coverson. Coverson. Coverson.
Across the lake. Yeah. Oh he was buried there.

Well no, they buried him, they buried him here because his wife's home is over there. And they buried him here I think. Because the last dance we played over there, before he was taking with that stroke, when we finished playing that night they'd bite the hole up. The people bite the hole up that night because I don't know they had some kind of trouble and we packed the place that night and went back the next time to play, they didn't have no hole in. Right there in Covers.
Well that night when you say Buddy took his stroke, was it after you'd finished the job? The first stroke or the second stroke.

The second stroke. Well he began to feel bad on the bandstand. And somehow or another that night he just knocked off and he couldn't finish the job. And he went home? And he went home, his wife was staying over there. And when we got off we went to see, found out how he was feeling, whether he couldn't talk at all then.
So what about his first stroke, Sammy? Did he take that on the bandstand?

Well he took that on the bandstand playing and his hand started to cramp him up, you know, cramp him up on him. And some of the boys went home and asked him what was his trouble and he told him his hands was, and he could hardly, his lip had turned a little bit. And they rushed him to the doctor and there was a stroke he had. Then he stopped playing for about a month, a little bit more than that, and then he started feeling good, because he's a fellow who used to like to play. He'd play if he could. And he felt better and then he started playing again. Well that next one, that was all of it.
How much, how far apart were those two strokes? A couple of years?
Oh it must have been about two or three years, because he lived a long time after the Foyceman. He did a lot of playing after the Foyceman.

Well yeah, I keep ending up this on a sad note, but I'm asking about these people because we never knew them. Zeb, do you know when did he die about? Was that before Buddy Petty or after, did you think?
Yes, Mr. Bill, Zeb died first. Before Buddy.
Yeah. I think Buddy died about 1931 I believe the date was.
Yeah, Zeb died first, because Zeb used to play with us, you know.
I never knew anybody much that knew anything about Zeb. Yeah.
But I didn't know no more than that about him. His name, I don't know.
He didn't know what part of town, or if he was born here in town, did you ever hear him
say anything about his life? Well I think he was born here in town because the head trumpet player used to be in the band, used to teach for y'all. Lewis the Man.
Lewis the Man.

Lewis the Man. He used to live right close to Lewis the Man, right in the back of Lewis the Man. I think he was born and raised right here. Up in that section. I think that was about on 6th Street or 7th Street or something like that. That's right.

That's right. Maybe 3rd or 4th, anyway it was up in that section. It said it around a little bit. If I haven't any other questions to ask, is there something else you can think of that you'd like to add about your life?
Well, Mr. Bill, I think that's about all I know. I think you covered it very well actually. Right now, because I forgot so much. I remember a lot of it. You know how it is years ago like that.
Did you ever play out in Mellon Boy?
Yes, I used to play out there with Alfre, Professor Alfre, the old man Alfre. Poise's daddy.
Willie? Willie.

You played with that player? I used to play with Willie and I used to play with the other brother too, he used to play. The saxophone. The saxophone. Yeah. He's playing now. Young Willie. Yeah, the old man and him. I mean we used to play together but Percy and him, at that time, we wasn't working, I was working with the old man.
I think Percy was a drummer for a while too, wasn't he? We haven't interviewed him. We interviewed the old man Willie and the young Willie too.
Yeah. Did you know his brother Earl? Did you know his brother Earl? Oh yeah, the tramont player? Yeah, I know him too. I know him.
What about those Milenburg things? Were they good fun?

Well it was a lot of fun because they used to have so many bands out there on Sunday till you just get up and walk to the gallery and just listen to another band playing they could do it to you. And both bands was fighting hard you know. It was very fun. Yes it was fun. Did you use the heavy sticks on those? Oh yeah you had to because they had so many bands around you know. You wanted to be heard you know. When you were bucking you used the heavy sticks?
Oh yeah I grabbed the heavy sticks.
Did you take them both with you on the job like that?
Oh yeah. I used to have them.

That was fun those days when Milenburg was running because you'd go out on a Sunday evening and you'd just know you were going to be around three and four bands out there playing different pavilions. There was a lot of kicks. And that music sounds so good going on the water you know. It sounds good. I used to be out there.
And you never played at the Miracle Round? Yeah, the Miracle Round, yes.
The Miracle Round. On Hickory Street?
That's, I don't know. Hickory and there.
Yes I played there. I played there after they had a parade for some club to give a dance there one Sunday. Tilma was playing with us. Wilma Tilma?
Yeah. Is that the same clubhouse they have down here now? It doesn't have any building on it. It's open? Oh right now, I'm playing open.

Years back we used to play at the San Suu, you know, you remember the San Suu Hall? Yeah. How about that? Well we played there many times too, Randy and Buddy P.T. played the heavy bands there all the time. That's old time, that's a long time ago you know. That hall's still there.
Yeah but they don't have any more dancers there.
No.
I walked in there, it's a pool, they got pool tables in there. The hall looks in good shape here. Yeah. Good cypress.
Right back in there.
Yeah, right back in that courtyard there. Yeah that's right. That's right. Looks in good shape here. You never have played at Booker Hill?
No I don't remember playing there. That's the Calton section.
No. By the river. I've heard Johnny St. Cyr talk about that.
By the Bunch of Hills. Yeah. No I knew. Did you play there Manuel?
Too young. Too young.

There's one thing the other day you mentioned, you'll ask Manuel Paul a little bit about his playing with Celestan, you mentioned that you made a movie with him. I think we might put that on the thing.

Yes, I made a picture with him at the old Absinthe House. That was the Cinorama Holiday I believe. That's right, that's right. With the big three dimension screen. Yeah, it's taken us about 12 hours to make that picture. Really? About 12 hours. It's a good movie alright. And that's the hardest job, that's the hardest job I have ever had in my life. Did you play with Celestan otherwise much? Well I did play off and on as a spare man, extra man. Whenever someone, when he'd need a saxophone player, I'd play with him. Where'd go he'd make trips, I'd go with him. Battleroy, to this place here in Georgia, Columbus, Georgia. Made trips out there with him. And also to this place they have, I can't think of the name of this place, it's on the West Bank. Good as I know it, I can't... Is it Alexandria or any place up there? No, it's not Alexander. Appaloosa. Oh. Yeah, Appaloosa, yes. I played up there with him. And many times before he formed this last band, I rehearsed with him, to help him get up the band. But I dropped out. Yeah. I dropped out.
Was there any other point that you forgot to tell us the other day that you wanted to make a note of?

Well, there were many things that I couldn't think of at the time, but even though now, I couldn't think of them. Because there were so many things that happened and... That's right, everybody played with almost everyone else I did. I can't remember the different bands I played. I played with every musician in the city. That's the bone, yeah. That's right, what I've done. I played with them. I played banjo with them. Oh, yeah. I played saxes, alto saxes with them. I played tenor with them. Mm-hmm. See? So those things, you will forget them. Yeah. But I think Sammy Pins have... He did very well to remember.
Yeah, I think you did too. I mean, there's nothing else you want to add? We'll just... Well...
No, Mr. Bill, I... I just about... I think I remembered all about doing the time. I think it's very well to go.

Thank you very well. Just before I... We might mention who you're working for. You've been working for the same place for many years, haven't you, Sammy? What place you mean? The same place you're working at now?
You mean music?
No, I mean...
Oh, I've been with the security storage company for 14 years now.
Mm-hmm. Well, how long have you been married about before you started?
Well, what I did, you see, I got... By the time I got married I went and got a job, because I used to work. I remember playing music, you see.
Was that your first job? This...
No, my first job was at OK Storage. Uh-huh.
And you were there long?
Well, I stayed there about, say, about ten years or something like that. Mm-hmm. And then? Then I went over here.

And then you went to the... I just wanted to sort of fix the date when you got married so it would fix it for your Chicago thing. Oh, yeah. About 24 years or something like that. Something like that. Where's the memory of the place you're working now?
Security.
Yeah. Just those are the two main jobs. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. All right, so I just wanted to get that... Yeah, I think that covers everything pretty well.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
